q: Vectors can be multiplied in two different ways: the scalar product and the vector product.
e: This is the exact definition provided in the textbook for vector multiplication.

q: Vectors can be multiplied in three different ways: the scalar product, the vector product, and the tensor product.
e: The textbook states vectors can be multiplied in two different ways: the scalar product and the vector product.

q: In the scalar product, a scalar can be formed by multiplying two vectors.
e: The scalar product results in a scalar quantity from two vectors.

q: In the scalar product, a vector can be formed by multiplying two vectors.
e: The scalar product forms a scalar, not a vector, when multiplying two vectors.

q: The scalar product of vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is defined as $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB \cos \theta$.
e: This is the standard mathematical definition of the scalar (dot) product.

q: The scalar product of vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is defined as $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB \sin \theta$.
e: The scalar product uses $\cos \theta$, while the vector product uses $\sin \theta$.

q: In the equation $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB \cos \theta$, $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
e: $\theta$ represents the angle between the two vectors being multiplied.

q: The scalar product is also called the dot product.
e: Scalar product and dot product are interchangeable terms in the textbook.

q: The scalar product is also called the cross product.
e: The scalar product is called the dot product; the vector product is called the cross product.

q: Work is the scalar product of force and displacement.
e: Although force and displacement are vectors, their scalar product (work) is a scalar.

q: Work is the vector product of force and displacement.
e: Work is the scalar product of force and displacement, not the vector product.

q: The scalar product has the commutative property as described by $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = \vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}$.
e: The order of vectors in a scalar product does not change the result.

q: The vector product of vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is defined as $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{C}$.
e: This is the standard definition of the vector (cross) product.

q: The magnitude of $\vec{C}$ in the vector product $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{C}$ is $C = AB \cos \theta$.
e: The magnitude of the vector product is $C = AB \sin \theta$.

q: The direction of $\vec{C}$ in a vector product is determined by using the right-hand rule.
e: The right-hand rule is explicitly used to find the direction of the cross product.

q: The direction of $\vec{C}$ is parallel to the plane that contains $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
e: The direction of $\vec{C}$ is perpendicular to the plane that contains $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.

q: The result of the vector product is a vector quantity.
e: Unlike the scalar product, the vector product yields a vector.

q: The vector product between two vectors is denoted by a cross ($\times$), hence this product is called the cross product.
e: The cross symbol denotes the vector product.

q: The vector product obeys the commutative property as $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{B} \times \vec{A}$.
e: The vector product does not obey the commutative property; $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$.

q: The formulae for the torque and the angular velocity are determined by using the vector product.
e: Torque and angular velocity relationships rely on the vector (cross) product.

q: To use the right-hand rule, first you have to hold up your right hand so that index finger and middle finger are perpendicular to thumb.
e: This is the exact physical description of setting up the right-hand rule.

q: In the right-hand rule, your index finger points in the direction of $\vec{B}$ and your middle finger points in the direction of $\vec{A}$.
e: The index finger points in the direction of $\vec{A}$ and the middle finger points in the direction of $\vec{B}$.

q: In the right-hand rule, your thumb will point in the direction of the cross product $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$.
e: The thumb indicates the resulting direction of the vector product.

q: When a force is applied to an object, it can turn the object about a certain point known as the pivot or the fulcrum.
e: The pivot or fulcrum is the point about which the turning effect occurs.

q: The turning effect of a force about a particular fulcrum is measured by the moment of that force or torque.
e: Moment of force and torque are the measures of the turning effect.

q: Torque is a scalar quantity.
e: Torque is a vector quantity, as it has both magnitude and direction.

q: The vector form of torque can be expressed as $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$.
e: Torque is the cross product of the position vector and the force vector.

q: The direction of torque is parallel to both $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$.
e: The direction of torque is perpendicular to both $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$.

q: The magnitude of the moment of force or torque $\tau$ is defined as the product of the force $F$ and the perpendicular distance $d$ from the line of action of the force to the fulcrum.
e: This is the exact definition of the magnitude of torque.

q: The equation for the magnitude of torque is $\tau = Fr \cos \theta = Fd$.
e: The correct equation for the magnitude of torque is $\tau = Fr \sin \theta = Fd$.

q: The perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the fulcrum ($d = r \sin \theta$) is also called the moment arm of a force.
e: The moment arm is specifically the perpendicular distance to the fulcrum.

q: The line of action of a force is a line along which a force is considered to act.
e: This is the textbook definition of the line of action of a force.

q: If a force acting on the object is at an angle of $90^{\circ}$, $r$ equals zero.
e: If the force is at $90^{\circ}$, $r$ equals $d$ (the moment arm equals the distance).

q: In SI units, the moment of force or torque is measured in newton metre (N m).
e: Newton metre is the correct SI unit for torque.

q: The unit newton metre (N m) for torque can be interchangeably written as joule.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the unit newton metre for torque is never written as joule.

q: The tangential acceleration of a particle rotating about an axis is $a = r\alpha$.
e: Tangential acceleration is the product of radius and angular acceleration.

q: According to Newton's second law, the force on a rotating particle is $F = ma = mr\omega$.
e: According to Newton's second law for rotation, $F = ma = mr\alpha$.

q: The torque due to tangential force is $\tau = Fr = (mr\alpha)r = mr^2\alpha$.
e: This derivation shows the relationship between torque, mass, radius, and angular acceleration.

q: In the equation $\tau = I\alpha$, the term $I = mr$ is the moment of inertia of that particle about the axis.
e: The moment of inertia of a particle is $I = mr^2$, not $mr$.

q: The moment of inertia of an object composed of particles is $I = m_1r_1^2 + m_2r_2^2 + \dots + m_nr_n^2 = \sum mr^2$.
e: This is the summation formula for the moment of inertia of a system of particles.

q: The moment of inertia of an object is defined as the sum of the products obtained by multiplying the mass of each particle in a given object and its distance from the axis.
e: It is the product of the mass and the square of its distance from the axis, not just the distance.

q: The moment of inertia is a scalar quantity.
e: Unlike torque or angular momentum, moment of inertia has no direction.

q: The SI unit of moment of inertia is kg m.
e: The SI unit of moment of inertia is kg m$^2$.

q: The moment of inertia must be specified with respect to a chosen axis of rotation.
e: Moment of inertia changes depending on the axis of rotation.

q: The moment of inertia for a hoop or cylindrical shell is $I = MR^2$.
e: This is the standard formula for a hoop or cylindrical shell.

q: The moment of inertia for a long thin rod with rotation axis through end is $I = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$.
e: For a rod rotating about its end, the moment of inertia is $I = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$.

q: The moment of inertia for a solid cylinder or disk is $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$.
e: This is the correct formula for a solid cylinder or disk.

q: The moment of inertia for a long thin rod with rotation axis through center is $I = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$.
e: For a rod rotating about its center, the moment of inertia is $I = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$.

q: The moment of inertia for a solid sphere is $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$.
e: This is the standard formula for a solid sphere.

q: The centre of gravity of a particular object is a point at which all its weight may be considered to act.
e: This is the exact definition of the centre of gravity.

q: For an object of regular shape and uniform density, the centre of gravity is at its geometrical center.
e: Uniform density and regular shape ensure the centre of gravity aligns with the geometrical center.

q: The weight of a metre stick of uniform density is considered to be acting at the 0 cm mark.
e: The weight of a uniform metre stick is considered to be acting at the 50 cm mark (its mid-point).

q: When the system is in static equilibrium, there is no linear motion and no rotational motion.
e: Static equilibrium requires the absence of both linear and rotational motion.

q: The conditions of static equilibrium are that the resultant force on the system is zero ($\sum F = 0$) and the resultant torque on the system is zero ($\sum \tau = 0$).
e: Both net force and net torque must be zero for static equilibrium.

q: The conditions of static equilibrium are that the resultant force on the system is zero ($\sum F = 0$) and the resultant torque on the system is maximum.
e: For static equilibrium, the resultant torque must also be zero, not maximum.

q: The condition necessary for a pivoted object to be in balance is given by the principle of moments.
e: The principle of moments governs the balance of pivoted objects.

q: The principle of moments states that if an object is to be in balance, the total clockwise moment about the fulcrum must equal the total anticlockwise moment.
e: This is the exact statement of the principle of moments.

q: The principle of moments states that if an object is to be in balance, the total clockwise moment about the fulcrum must be greater than the total anticlockwise moment.
e: The total clockwise moment must equal, not be greater than, the total anticlockwise moment.

q: Examples of the application of the principle of moments include building site crane and beam balance.
e: These are explicitly listed as applications of the principle of moments.

q: In rotational motion, the angular momentum of an object is defined as the product of its moment of inertia and the angular velocity.
e: This is the fundamental definition of angular momentum.

q: In rotational motion, the angular momentum of an object is defined as the product of its mass and the angular velocity.
e: Angular momentum is the product of moment of inertia and angular velocity, not mass and angular velocity.

q: The equation for angular momentum is $L = I\omega$.
e: $L = I\omega$ is the standard formula for angular momentum.

q: The moment of inertia is analogous to mass in linear motion.
e: Moment of inertia plays the same role in rotational motion as mass does in linear motion.

q: The angular velocity is analogous to the linear acceleration in linear motion.
e: Angular velocity is analogous to linear velocity, not linear acceleration.

q: The SI unit of angular momentum is kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$.
e: Derived from kg m$^2$ (moment of inertia) and rad s$^{-1}$ (angular velocity).

q: Angular momentum is a scalar quantity.
e: Angular momentum is a vector quantity, possessing both magnitude and direction.

q: The law of conservation of angular momentum states that if there is no net external torque acting on an isolated system, the total angular momentum of the system is constant.
e: This is the exact statement of the law of conservation of angular momentum.

q: The law of conservation of angular momentum states that if there is a net external torque acting on an isolated system, the total angular momentum of the system is constant.
e: The law applies only when there is no net external torque acting on the system.

q: In symbols, if $\sum \tau = 0$, then $L = \text{constant}$.
e: Zero net torque implies constant angular momentum.

q: An example of conservation of angular momentum is seen in an ice skater performing a spin.
e: The ice skater spin is the classic textbook example of this conservation law.

q: An ice skater's angular momentum is conserved because the net torque on her is very large.
e: Her angular momentum is conserved because the net torque on her is very small (negligible).

q: An ice skater's rate of spin increases greatly as her moment of inertia decreases by pulling in her arms inwards.
e: Decreasing moment of inertia requires an increase in angular speed to conserve angular momentum.

q: If an ice skater wants to slow down her rotation, she will pull her arms inwards.
e: To slow down, she must stretch her arms outwards to increase her moment of inertia.

q: When her moment of inertia increases, the rotational angular speed will decrease.
e: This is the direct consequence of the conservation of angular momentum.

q: A springboard diver who is rotating when jumping off the board needs to make continuous physical effort to continue rotating.
e: The diver does not need to make any physical effort to continue rotating due to conservation of angular momentum.

q: The application of conservation of angular momentum can be used to determine the angular velocity of a rotating system in which the moment of inertia is changing.
e: This is a primary practical application of the conservation law.
